title: Summary of 2022-23 Winter Season Operations and Evaluation: Southern and Central Utah Cloud Seeding Program
authors: North American Weather Consultants (NAWC) for Utah Division of Water Resources
finding: the precipitation evaluation results are strongest mathematically, and suggest a 1.2-1.5 inch increase in seasonal precipitation in the target areas due to seeding. This would likely produce an average additional runoff of more than 70,000 acre-feet annually in these watersheds.
strengthWhy: Same state, same agency, same mechanism (operational winter orographic seeding), runoff expressed in acre-feet; but this is the central/southern Utah target, not the Great Salt Lake tributary basins
differencesFromUtah: Within Utah, but target areas drain to the Sevier/Colorado systems rather than to Great Salt Lake; GSL-basin programme (Northern Utah) is a separate, smaller target

title: Summary of 2021-22 Winter Season Operations and Evaluation: Northern Utah Cloud Seeding Program
authors: North American Weather Consultants (NAWC); sponsored by Bear River Water Conservancy District and Utah Division of Water Resources
place: Cache and Box Elder Counties, northern Utah (Bear River basin, Great Salt Lake tributary)
publisher: Utah Division of Water Resources / Idaho Water Resource Board document library
finding: A 2012 study estimated a total (average) seasonal increase of approximately 56,000 acre-feet from the seeding program.
strengthWhy: Same mechanism, same basin: operational ground-based winter seeding over Bear River basin mountains that drain to Great Salt Lake; figure is seasonal runoff-equivalent in acre-feet
differencesFromUtah: None substantive; it is the Great Salt Lake basin itself. Gain is the estimated gross runoff increase before upstream diversion/depletion, and estimate rests on target/control regression with wide 5-15% uncertainty

title: Does Efficient Irrigation Technology Lead to Reduced Groundwater Extraction? Empirical Evidence (AAEA selected paper; published version JEEM 67(2):189-208, 2014)
authors: Lisa Pfeiffer and C.-Y. Cynthia Lin
publisher: Agricultural and Applied Economics Association / AgEcon Search
finding: We find that increases in irrigation efficiency in western Kansas from 1995 to 2005 have led to increases in groundwater extraction, a rebound effect of over 100%. ... a 1% increase in the percentage of acres irrigated with dropped nozzle center pivot systems leads to a 1.7% increase in the amount of water extracted per farmed acre
conversion: A rebound effect >100% of nominal savings implies the real net water saved is zero or negative, i.e. an effective delivery share of 0 (not 0.55). Expressed as share of nominal savings that is a real reduction in extraction.
strengthWhy: Direct empirical measurement of the exact mechanism (subsidised on-farm efficiency upgrades) with metered extraction data, but measures groundwater pumping in a plains aquifer rather than surface-water depletion in a terminal-lake basin
differencesFromUtah: Groundwater-dominated High Plains irrigation with corn/soy; Utah GSL basin is surface-water dominated with alfalfa/hay, prior-appropriation rights and a lake endpoint. Kansas farmers had slack within allocations, allowing crop shifts that drove the rebound.

title: Phragmites Control and Restoration Strategy
authors: Utah Division of Forestry, Fire and State Lands (FFSL)
place: Great Salt Lake wetlands and lakebed, Utah
publisher: Utah Division of Forestry, Fire and State Lands
finding: It was estimated that under standard conditions Phragmites consumed, though ET, approximately 3.62 acre-ft of water per acre of Phragmites compared to 1.55 acre-ft of water per acre of Inland Saltgrass ... If there is approximately 30,000 acres of Phragmites in the wetlands of Great Salt Lake, removing 5,246 acres ... would reduce the amount of water lost through ET by 10%.
location: 'Phragmites Water Use and Impacts to Hydrology', pp. 1-2
conversion: Net ET saving = 3.62 - 1.55 = 2.07 acre-ft per acre converted to saltgrass; 30,000 acres x 2.07 = 62,100 acre-ft/yr if the entire GSL Phragmites stand were converted. A realistic programme cap is well below this, so the model's 50 KAF/yr sits near the physical ceiling of total eradication.
strengthWhy: Exact mechanism, exact place (Great Salt Lake delta/wetlands), agency estimate; but the per-acre ET figures are modelled, not measured - the document itself calls them 'theoretical' and notes empirical flux-tower work is still underway
differencesFromUtah: None - it is Utah/GSL. Caveat: ET saved in a lakebed wetland partly returns to the lake only if the freed water is not simply re-evaporated by replacement vegetation or open water.

title: Water Optimization Programs - presentation to the Natural Resources, Agriculture, and Environment Interim Committee
authors: Candice Hasenyager (Director, Utah Division of Water Resources) and Brett Bunker (Ag Optimization Committee Chair)
place: Utah (statewide, incl. Great Salt Lake basin)
finding: Saved Water and Water Use Impacts: 20 projects completed; Analysis is limited; No 'Saved water' change applications filed; Preliminary analysis - Diversion: potential for notable decreases; Depletion: negligible change expected.
location: Slide 'Saved Water and Water Use Impacts'
conversion: Utah's own programme reports large diversion reductions with 'negligible change expected' in depletion, i.e. the real consumptive-use share of nominal on-farm savings is near zero rather than 0.55.
strengthWhy: Same state, same programme type the model is representing (subsidised on-farm irrigation efficiency), stated by the administering agency; but it is a preliminary qualitative statement from a slide deck, with no measured acre-foot figure
differencesFromUtah: None - it is the Utah programme. Weakness: only 20 completed projects analysed and the agency flags the analysis as limited.
verification: WebFetch of PDF then pdftotext grep of the saved file

title: Colorado River System Conservation Pilot Program (Assistance Listing 15.567) - program results
authors: U.S. Bureau of Reclamation, Department of the Interior
place: Upper and Lower Colorado River Basin (incl. Utah)
finding: In 2017 there were 15 projects accomplished resulting in 11,408 acre-feet of consumptive use savings. In 2018 there were 19 projects accomplished resulting in 25,319 acre-feet of consumptive use savings.
conversion: Best single year of a voluntary, paid fallowing/deficit-irrigation programme across the whole Colorado Basin: 25,319 acre-feet = 25 KAF/yr. The model's 100 KAF/yr cap for the GSL basin is roughly 4x the best observed year of this much larger multi-state programme.
strengthWhy: Same mechanism (voluntary payments to fallow or switch to lower-water crops, measured as consumptive-use reduction) in the interior West, including Utah participants; but a different basin, short pilot, and funding-limited rather than capacity-limited
differencesFromUtah: Colorado River basin rather than GSL basin; conserved water went to Lake Powell storage with no shepherding mechanism; participation was capped by the $8.5M budget, so the figure is a budget cap, not a willingness ceiling

title: Utah saves farm water, but can't yet track how much reaches the Great Salt Lake
finding: State dashboard reports 'more than 125,000 acre-feet in reported water savings each year'; a source says '125,000 acre feet of diversion savings is still only like the first step' toward dedicating that water to the lake.
conversion: 125,000 acre-feet/yr of reported savings = 125 KAF/yr, but this is DIVERSION savings, not depletion. The model's 70 KAF/yr on-farm cap is plausible as a gross diversion figure; the real consumptive-use figure is unknown and the 2025 annual report found 'mixed results when looking at depletion changes in case studies'.
strengthWhy: Reports the actual Utah programme's cumulative annual reported savings; but it is journalism relaying a state dashboard, the unit is diversion not depletion, and the figure is cumulative across many projects over several years
differencesFromUtah: None geographically; the key mismatch is diversion vs depletion accounting and the state's admitted inability to trace water to the lake

title: Utah saves farm water, but can't yet track how much reaches the Great Salt Lake
finding: Officials and experts said they 'cannot point to a specific amount of the reported agricultural water savings' that reached the lake; the programme 'lacks the technology to see where the saved water goes'.
conversion: No number available: the administering agencies state the delivered share is currently unmeasured, so the model's 0.80 crop-switching delivery share is not supported by measurement in Utah.
strengthWhy: Directly about the delivery question in the right basin, but establishes absence of evidence rather than a value
